computer-vision: A wide, symmetrical illustration centered on a camera lens drawn as a machine's eye, mounted on a fingernail-sized chip powered by a small coin battery while a strip of live video frames streams into it, so the viewer sees at once that these models are compact, low-power, and fast enough to work in real time. Feeding the eye from the left is a towering archive of photographs, each stamped by a human hand with a label — person, stop sign, crack in a weld — the labeled training data from which the machine has statistically learned to correlate shapes, textures, and colors with words. The scene the eye currently sees is rendered as a grid of pixel patches, each patch carrying a cluster of competing confidence scores such as 92 percent truck, 7 percent bus, 1 percent other, making visible that vision's output is a set of probabilities rather than a certainty. From the eye, two identical recognition beams fan outward in opposite directions: one lands on a phone unlocking to its owner's face, a tractor scanning crop rows, and a car windshield reading the road ahead; the other lands on a missile and a drone bearing the very same eye inside a targeting reticle, with no human controller anywhere in the frame, a machine that can act on what it sees without asking anyone. The two beams are drawn in the same color and weight, the composition balances like a scale around the central lens, and a small caption beneath reads: the capability is neutral — everything depends on what it is pointed at.
edge-ai: A wide illustration in clean infographic style, divided into three zones that together tell the story of moving intelligence out of the cloud and into the device. The upper-left corner, washed out in grey, shows the old arrangement: a smartphone fires a thin dotted request line across a wide empty gap toward a distant glowing datacenter sitting in a network cloud, with the answer crawling back along a second line; the whole corner is stamped with a large faded X, and beside it a small stopwatch and a frayed, cut cable hint at the problems of delay, dead zones and dropped links. The dominant right side is bright and detailed: a cutaway view of a small delivery vehicle, its camera at the front and, immediately behind it inside the body, a tiny green circuit board bearing a chip stamped with a brain symbol; thought lines loop entirely within the vehicle as it reads a roadside sign, showing the decision happening locally, with no line leaving the box even though its network cable hangs severed. Along the bottom, a conveyor belt runs out of a factory puffing symbols of cheap mass production, spilling hundreds of identical brain-chips into plain boxes; four of the identical chips are shown slotted into their new homes — a warehouse robot scanning a shelf, a car windshield reading a speed-limit sign, a drone steadying itself in gusty wind, and a factory camera flagging a cracked part on an assembly line — while a fifth chip, drawn in exactly the same size and friendly style, sits in the guidance bay of a missile whose shipping manifest is a blank page marked only with a question mark, the image's one somber note that these parts are too numerous to trace and that the same component serves a robotics startup and a weapons program alike.
export-controls: A single tall illustration shaped like an hourglass, read from top to bottom. At the top, a fortified border checkpoint under a sign reading "EXPORT CONTROLS": a handful of enormous, gleaming datacenter accelerators sit in crates wrapped in chains and stamped with red "RESTRICTED" seals, while uniformed officials with clipboards and national flags turn shipping crates away; alongside them in the same guarded queue stand machine tools, drums of chemicals and crates of weapons, and a small vignette shows a smuggler being handcuffed for slipping a chip across the barrier. One crate labeled "legal to sell at home" stands visible in a domestic storefront, forbidden only at the fence. The few chips feed into a narrow neck where a single glowing file—the trained model—squeezes through under a customs officer's eye, a padlock sketched around it, labeled "training: scarce, expensive, watched." Below the neck the composition explodes outward: the file shatters into thousands of identical glowing icons that drift like seeds across a vast, fenceless plain, settling effortlessly onto mass-market hardware—laptops, phones, game consoles, consumer graphics cards, small office servers—in the hands of ordinary people worldwide, some using them for medicine, translation and teaching, others visibly scheming; borders here are only faint dotted lines the copies cross at will. The contrast is the whole argument: iron grip and scarcity at the top, abundance and total freedom at the bottom, where nearly all actual use happens.
